misconceptions.A1: Assigning one name to another makes an independent copy of the list.
misconceptions.A2: Two names for the same object are linked, so rebinding one name also moves the other.
misconceptions.A3: Two lists with equal contents are the same object.
misconceptions.A4: A function gets its own copy of what I pass, so changing it inside will not show outside.
misconceptions.A5: Assigning to a parameter name inside a function changes the caller's variable.
misconceptions.A6: Calling a string method like s.upper() changes s.
misconceptions.A7: x += 1 or s += 'a' changes the existing int or string.
misconceptions.A8: a += [1] and a = a + [1] do the same thing to a list.
misconceptions.A9: A tuple can never change, including what is inside it.

predictB.prompt: When the program finishes, which names refer to the same object?

options.text: a and b refer to the same list
a and b refer to two separate lists

steps.caption: A new list [1, 2] is created and the name a points to it.
b is a second name for the same list. No new list is created.
append changes the list in place. Both names point to that one list, so both see the change.
print(a) shows the list a points to.

feedback.correct: Right. There is only one list, and a and b are two names for it.

A1.thought: You may have pictured b = a as making a separate copy of the list, so changing b would leave a alone.
A1.why: That is a natural reading. In everyday life, writing down a value in a second place gives you a second copy.
A1.model: In Python, b = a makes b another name for the same list. There is still only one list, so appending through b changes what a sees.

predictB.prompt: When the program finishes, which names refer to the same object?

b is a second name for the same list.
A new list [9] is created and b is moved to point at it. a still points at the original list.
print(a) shows the list a points to, which was never changed.

feedback.correct: Right. Assigning to b only moves the name b. The list a points to is untouched.

A2.thought: You may have thought that after b = a the two names stay tied together, so giving b a new list moves a as well.
A2.why: Because b = a made them share a list, it is easy to treat the two names as linked.
A2.model: Names are labels, not links. b = [9] points b at a brand-new list, and a still points at the original [1, 2]. Only changing the shared list itself (like append) is seen through both names.

A2.why: After b = a it is easy to treat the names as linked, since changes through one showed up in the other.

snippets.title: Equal is not the same
snippets.preface: In Python, == asks whether two values have equal contents, and is asks whether two names refer to the very same object.

options.text: True False
True True
False False

predictB.prompt: When the program finishes, which names refer to the same object?

options.text: a and b refer to two separate lists that happen to be equal
a and b refer to the same list

steps.caption: A new list [1, 2] is created and a points to it.
Writing [1, 2] again creates a second, separate list. It has the same contents, but it is a different object.
a == b is True because the contents are equal. a is b is False because the names point at different objects.

feedback.correct: Right. The two lists are equal, but they are two separate objects.

A3.thought: You may have reasoned that two lists with the same contents are the same thing, so is would also say True.
A3.why: In everyday life, two identical-looking things are often treated as one. And == really does say True here.
A3.model: == compares contents. is asks whether two names point to the very same object. Writing [1, 2] twice creates two separate lists that happen to be equal.

snippets.title: Alias, copy, and equal
snippets.preface: In Python, == asks whether two values have equal contents, and is asks whether two names refer to the very same object. The expression a[:] makes a new list with the same items as a.
code: print(a == c, a is b, a is c)

options.text: True True False
True True True
True False False

predictB.prompt: When the program finishes, which names refer to the same object?

options.text: a and b refer to the same list, and c refers to a different list
a, b, and c all refer to the same list
a, b, and c each refer to their own list

steps.caption: A new list [1, 2] is created and a points to it.
b = a adds a second name for the same list. No copy is made.
a[:] builds a new list with the same items, and c points to that new list.
a == c is True (equal contents). a is b is True (same object). a is c is False (different objects).

feedback.correct: Right. b is another name for a's list, while c is a separate list that happens to be equal.

A1.thought: You may have pictured b = a as making a copy, so that a is b would be False.
A1.why: It is natural to expect an equals sign to copy, especially in a snippet that also contains a real copy.
A1.model: b = a makes no copy: a and b point at the same list. Only c = a[:] makes a new list.

A3.thought: You may have reasoned that c has the same contents as a, so it must be the same list.
A3.why: Equal contents make == True, and that can feel like the same thing as being identical.
A3.model: c = a[:] built a new list. It is equal to a, but it is a different object, so a is c is False.

feedback.correct: Right. upper() builds a new string and s = s.upper() moves only s to it. t still points to the original, because strings cannot be changed in place.

A6.why: A method call like upper() sounds like an action done to the string itself, the way append is done to a list, and with a list the alias would see the change.
A6.model: Strings cannot be changed in place. s.upper() builds a brand new string, "ABC", and the assignment moves only s to it. t still points to the original "abc".

options.text: lst and inner refer to the same list; t is a different object
all three names refer to different objects

steps.caption: The list [2, 3] is created and lst points to it.
The tuple holds the number 1 and a reference to the same list that lst points to. It does not copy the list.
t[1] is that same list, so inner is a third name for it.
append changes the list in place. The tuple's cells are untouched, but the list its second cell points to now holds three items.

feedback.correct: Right. The tuple holds a reference to the list, so lst and inner are the same list and the change shows through t.

A9.thought: You may have thought that because a tuple cannot change, the list inside it is frozen too, so t and inner would keep [2, 3] while only lst became [2, 3, 4].
A9.why: Tuples do reject item assignment, so it is natural to treat everything inside one as frozen.
A9.model: A tuple's cells are fixed: they always point at the same objects. But the list in the second cell is a mutable object, and it is the very list lst points to. lst.append(4) changes it, so t shows [2, 3, 4], and so does inner.

A1.thought: You may have thought inner = t[1] makes a copy of the list, so inner would keep [2, 3] while the tuple and lst show the change.
A1.why: Assignment can feel like copying, so it is natural to expect inner to be its own list.
A1.model: No copy is made. t[1] is the same list that lst points to, so inner = t[1] gives a third name for that list. Appending through lst shows up through t and inner alike.
